newsitem.title: UK: UK-US air deal not expected before next year.
newsitem.headline: UK-US air deal not expected before next year.

text.p: U.S. and British transport officials started a three-day session of open skies talks in London on Wednesday aimed at freeing up Europe's biggest transatlantic market for air traffic.

But industry sources said officials immediately made clear no deal was likely this year as their hands were tied until the British competition authorities ruled on British Airways' planned alliance with American Airlines.

Britain's trade and industry minister Ian Lang referred the matter back last month for further deliberation by his Office of Fair Trading (OFT) and industry sources say no decision is now expected from Lang before the new year.

"The (government negotiators) made the point, and the British side particularly, that nothing was going to be decided until the OFT had given its recommendation," said one airline observer attending the opening round of talks today.
"Our understanding is that the overall timetable for the talks is likely to mirror the regulatory timetable for (considering approval of) the alliance," said another source.

That meant the rest of this week's session was likely to be confined to negotiating about smaller technical matters rather than the main issues which have been in dispute for over five years, said an official with one airline.
"So we are probably looking at another couple of months rather than couple of days, with the meatier, more exciting issues probably left towards the end of the process," he said.
"It's more a case of the peripheral issues being discussed at the moment and how could that be any different until (Lang) makes his decision?" said a source close to the talks.
Lang's ruling on the BA/American alliance was due in September, after he received the results of an initial three-month investigation into the deal by the OFT.
There has been industry speculation that the OFT advised him the deal should be blocked by referring it for a lengthy investigation by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.

But, pressed by a Cabinet split on the issue, Lang decided instead to postpone the matter by asking the OFT to seek concessions from BA and American such as giving up runway slots at London Heathrow to make way for competition, sources said.
"The government has filed this one in the "too difficult to decide' cupboard," said an executive at one airline.
BA has refused to give up slots, saying other carriers have a bigger share of slots at their home hubs and should find their own slots through trading and normal allocations at Heathrow.
Under the proposed alliance BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week to 22 U.S. destinations with American's 238 flights from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

BA and American have argued their deal will lead to greater competition because it will only go ahead if Britain and the United States agree open skies, allowing all U.S. airlines access to Heathrow, the most popular of Europe's transatlantic landfalls.
Under the current aviation agreement dating back to March 1991 only British Airways, Virgin Atlantic Airways, American and United Ailrines are allowed to use Heathrow.

But open skies talks broke down in August amidst complaints by U.S. carriers that Heathrow is so crowded that open access would be meaningless unless they were to be granted some of British Airways' 38 percent share of slots.

The talks also stuck on demands by Virgin for so-called "cabotage" rights to allow it to fly domestic U.S. routes, in return for allowing U.S. carriers "fifth freedom" rights to fly on from Britain into mainland Europe.
Virgin denied on Wednesday recent media reports that suggested it would settle for being allowed to have franchised services in the United States, operated by a U.S. carrier.
"That idea was a complete plant (in the media)," company spokesman Will Whitehorn said.
"We don't think franchising offers us anything. We want to operate services ourselves in the United States."
